Courses/Docker from the kernel up

Puzzle 9 · 10 of 17

What is inside an image?

Module 1 treated an image as "the files a container starts from". Here's what an image really is on disk, file by file, and how one small change becomes part of a new image without copying the rest.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 3: A file tree of its own

    A mount attaches a set of files to a folder in the one tree that starts at /. A mount namespace gives its processes their own list of mounts, so a mount made inside is invisible outside. Docker uses one to mount the image's files at /, the container's root filesystem: the container sees the image's files, and the host's only if you mount them in.

The problem

Puzzle 3 showed Docker mounting an image's files at /, and puzzle 0 said ten containers from one image are ten processes. But an image isn't one folder of files. alpine:3.20 downloaded as 3.6 MB and takes 12.2 MB on disk; an image that adds one file to Alpine doesn't download Alpine again. And a container can delete a file, yet the image it came from never changes. So what is an image made of?

See it

The building block

docker save writes an image into one tar archive (tar is a format that packs many files, with their names and permissions, into one file, and also the program that packs and unpacks it), so you can open it and look. Inside, each piece of the image is a blob: one file under blobs/sha256/. For alpine:3.20 on the run behind this page:

$ docker save alpine:3.20 -o alpine.tar && mkdir img && tar -xf alpine.tar -C img && find img -type f | sort
img/blobs/sha256/25f1d6b1951ac8eb3740558fe94cb83d377bdadf95fd9f98b50d2e1b96130471
img/blobs/sha256/3a030ca3f633…   (7 more small files under blobs/sha256)
img/index.json
img/manifest.json
img/oci-layout

Seven of the eight blobs are JSON files, from a few hundred bytes to 73 kB. One is 3,630,321 bytes of gzip-compressed data (squeezed smaller, like a .zip). Unpack it and it is itself a tar archive of 517 entries: bin/, bin/busybox, bin/cat and the rest of Alpine. That archive is a layer: a set of file changes, packed as a tar. Alpine's only layer adds every file, because it starts from nothing.

The next layer starts from something. On the run behind this page, a container from alpine:3.20, called edit, ran a shell that wrote /notes.txt and deleted /etc/motd, then exited. docker diff lists what it changed, and docker commit turns those changes into a new image, notes:v1:

$ docker diff edit
A /notes.txt
C /etc
D /etc/motd
$ docker commit edit notes:v1
sha256:6b8731de370cb2444f1fa5df09bd9342f56c4d2d0a79ed346e0e603a7eca4663
$ docker history notes:v1
IMAGE          CREATED                  CREATED BY                                      SIZE      COMMENT
6b8731de370c   Less than a second ago   sh -c echo hello > /notes.txt; rm /etc/motd     12.3kB
d9e853e87e55   7 months ago             CMD ["/bin/sh"]                                 0B        buildkit.dockerfile.v0
<missing>      7 months ago             ADD alpine-minirootfs-3.20.10-x86_64.tar.gz …   8.47MB    buildkit.dockerfile.v0

notes:v1 is Alpine's layer, unchanged, plus one new layer of 12.3 kB. (The middle line made no layer: it only changed a setting, as its 0B says.) Saved and unpacked, the new layer holds exactly three entries:

drwxr-xr-x 0/0               0 2026-11-22 22:15 etc/
---------- 0/0               0 1970-01-01 00:00 etc/.wh.motd
-rw-r--r-- 0/0               6 2026-11-22 22:15 notes.txt

notes.txt is the added file. The deletion is the interesting one: a tar archive can't contain "the absence of a file", so the layer holds an empty file named .wh.motd. That is a whiteout: a file whose name says "delete motd from the layers below". When the layers are stacked (puzzle 10), the whiteout hides /etc/motd. The bytes of motd are still in layer 1, so deleting a file in a later layer never makes an image smaller.

Last, the image config: one of the small JSON files. For alpine:3.20 it says, among other things:

"config": { "Env": ["PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin"],
            "Cmd": ["/bin/sh"], "WorkingDir": "/" },
"rootfs": { "type": "layers",
            "diff_ids": ["sha256:08bc4e534116aa76b16015484b82eac51f9a593416feae9296c8a2d4bb7aa4a2"] }

Cmd is the program a container runs when docker run names none: that's why docker run alpine:3.20 gives you a shell. rootfs lists the layers, bottom first, each by a long name that puzzle 13 explains; notes:v1's config lists two. docker commit also writes the container's command into the new config, so notes:v1's Cmd is sh -c "echo hello > /notes.txt; rm /etc/motd", not /bin/sh. That's why the next puzzles always name a program, as in docker run notes:v1 sleep 1000. The remaining small files tie a config and its layers together for downloading; puzzles 15 and 16 open them.

So an image is: an ordered stack of layers, and a config. Usually layers come from a Dockerfile (Module 3, coming soon), not from docker commit, but each step still records only what changed.

The analogy

The flat's furniture arrives as a stack of delivery notes, oldest at the bottom. The first note lists everything for an empty flat. Each later note lists only changes: "add a desk", and for a removal, a slip that says "take away the old lamp". The lamp isn't collected; the slip just says nobody should see it. On top of the stack sits a card with the house rules: what the tenant does first on moving in, and which notes, in which order, make the flat.

Run it yourself

On a Linux machine with Docker. Before the last command, predict how many entries the new layer has and what the deletion looks like.

docker run --name edit alpine:3.20 sh -c "echo hello > /notes.txt; rm /etc/motd"
docker diff edit
docker commit edit notes:v1
docker history notes:v1
mkdir n && docker save notes:v1 | tar -x -C n
for f in n/blobs/sha256/*; do tar -tvf "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -q notes.txt && tar -tvf "$f"; done
docker rm edit

The loop looks inside every blob that is a tar archive (gzip-compressed or not) and prints the one that holds notes.txt. With Docker's older way of storing images (puzzle 12) the layers are saved uncompressed, under a different name (puzzle 13). Output from the run behind this page, last command:

drwxr-xr-x 0/0               0 2026-11-22 22:15 etc/
---------- 0/0               0 1970-01-01 00:00 etc/.wh.motd
-rw-r--r-- 0/0               6 2026-11-22 22:15 notes.txt

Keep notes:v1: the next puzzles use it.

Check yourself

A container from notes:v1 deletes /notes.txt, and you commit it as notes:v3. How many layers does notes:v3 have, and how big is the new one?

Right. Each commit adds a layer of changes; deleting hides, never removes.

Not quite. The bytes stay in layer 2; the whiteout only hides them.

Not quite. Layers only add on top; a deletion is a new layer with a whiteout.

A 500 MB file is added in one layer and deleted in the next. Roughly how much does pulling the image download for it?

Right. Deleting later doesn't take bytes out of earlier layers.

Not quite. Layers are stored and moved separately, in order.

Not quite. The whiteout hides the file in the merged view; layer 1's bytes still travel.

You start a container from notes:v1 without naming a program. What does it run, and where does that choice come from?

Not quite. docker commit records the container's command as the new image's Cmd.

Right. Layers hold files; the config holds how to run, and commit rewrote it.

Not quite. The new config keeps a Cmd: the container's own command.

  • OCI image spec v1.1.1: Image Configuration ("A layer DiffID is the digest over the layer's uncompressed tar archive")

  • Docker docs: docker container commit ("Create a new image from a container's changes")
  • Docker docs: docker image save ("Save one or more images to a tar archive (streamed to STDOUT by default)")

What you now know

An image is an ordered stack of layers plus an image config. Each layer is a tar archive of file changes; a deletion is stored as an empty whiteout file, .wh.<name>, so the deleted bytes stay in the layer below. The config says how to run the image and lists its layers in order.
